```{r load-data, include=TRUE}
# load data 
seoul_bikes_raw <- read_csv("data/SeoulBikeData.csv", locale=locale(encoding="latin1"))
#extracting raw data, locale needed to be specified as error otherwise.

#clean data
seoul_bikes <- seoul_bikes_raw |> 
  clean_names() |> #cleaning names to snake_case, as column headings' words initially separated with space
  select(-functioning_day)
```


## Introduction

In this project, we will be analysing the demand for rented bikes in Seoul, with the aims of **predicting the demand for rented bikes in Seoul considering time and weather variables.** This predictive model will be useful for helping to maintain a stable supply for bike renters, as well as help rented bike companies to project revenues in the future.

## Data

### Raw Dataset

The Seoul rented bikes data set has 8760 observations across 14 features. Each observation records details of the date, hourly bike demand, hour of day, temperature, rainfall, snowfall and other time and weather related-variables.

### Cleaning

In the raw data set, a variable called functioning_day was used to signify if the bike-renting system was operational or not. We realised that when functioning_day == "no," all instances of rented_bike_count had a value of 0. As we are interested in the number of rented bikes, this would not be relevant for our goal.

We also used clean_names() to ensure that all variables have in snake_case for simplicity when writing code.

### Feature Engineering

We ultimately engineered three variables, but one of which will not be used in our linear model, which will be explained in later sections of this report.

precipitation — has values 1 or 0, used to indicate if there was any forms of rainfall or snowfall.

is_weekend — determines if the day is a weekday or during the weekend.

peak — determines if the hour of day is a peak commuting time. We have defined this to be 7-9am and 5-7pm. This is the engineered variable that will be removed after exploratory data analysis (EDA).
seoul
### Key Predictors

For our model the following variables are what we will consider: rented_bike_count, hour, holiday, is_weekend, temperature_c, humidity_percent, seasons and precipitation.

Below is a variable table of the clean data:


| Variable Name | Type | Description |
|:--- | :--- |:--- |
| rented_bike_count | numerical | number of bikes rented per hour |
| hour | categorical | describes the hour of day, categorical data as it will be used as a factor |
| holiday | categorical | determines if the day is a holiday or not |
| is_weekend | categorical | determines if it is a day in the week or in the weekend |
| temperature_c | numerical | temperature of Seoul in degrees Celsius |
| humidity_percent | numerical | humidity of Seoul in percent |
| seasons | categorical | determines if the day is in winter, spring, summer or autumn |
| precipitation | numerical | has values 1 or 0 used to determine if there was any precipitation during the hour of day |

## Initial Findings

### Temperature vs. Number of Rented Bikes in Specific Time Windows

```{r, message = FALSE, echo = FALSE, fig.width = 10, fig.height = 4.5, out.width = "100%"}
seoul_bikes <- seoul_bikes |> 
  mutate(
    peak = ifelse(hour %in% c(7:9, 17:19), TRUE, FALSE)
    #used Gemini to help with shortening the conditional statement, as initially was hour == 7 | hour == 8 | ... 
  )

seoul_bikes |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = temperature_c, y = rented_bike_count)) +
  geom_jitter(
    aes(colour = peak),
    alpha = 0.15
  ) +
  geom_smooth(
    method = "gam",
    se = FALSE,
    linewidth = 1.2,
    colour = "#d95f02"
    ) +
  facet_grid( #changed to facet_grid to take holidays into account, not taking weekdays vs. weekends into account as there many weekend workers in Seoul who may need to commute
    holiday ~ peak,
    labeller = as_labeller(c("TRUE" = "Peak", "FALSE" = "Non-Peak", "Holiday" = "Holiday", "No Holiday" = "Working Day"))
    ) +
  #changes labels from facetting to "Peak" and "Non-Peak"
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    panel.spacing.x = unit(1.5, "cm") # Increases horizontal gap between the two columns
  ) +
  scale_colour_manual(
    guide = "legend",
    values = c("TRUE" = "#384860", "FALSE" = "#97a6c4"), #changed colour to lighter shades, as otherwise points are too dark
    labels = c("TRUE" = "Peak", "FALSE" = "Non-Peak")
    ) +
  guides(alpha = "none") +
  labs(
    x = "Temperature (c)",
    y = "Number of Rented Bikes Per Hour",
    colour = "Peak Commuting Hour (7-9am or 5-7pm)",
    title = "Bike Demand vs. Temperature"
  )
```

In the graph above, we first see that no matter the time period or day (i.e holiday vs. non-holiday), that the demanded for rented bikes increases as temperatures increases, with its optimal range at approximately 25-28°C.

After that range, demand begins to drop off.

Additionally, demand is substantially higher during peak hours on working days, vs. non-peak hours on working days, as they have maximum values of approximately 3600 versus 2600 rented bikes at their peaks.

However, this gap disappears on holidays, where the maximum values for rented bike demand during peak and non-peak hours are within the range of 2200-2400 rented bikes.

```{r, echo = FALSE}    
determine_density_maxes <- function(df, max_var, max_var_condition, density_var){ #parameters to keep generality of function
  density_df <- df |>
    filter({{ max_var }} == max_var_condition) |>
    pull({{ density_var }}) |> 
    density() |> 
    (\(d) tibble::tibble(x = d$x, y = d$y))()
    #creating a separate data frame for density values
  
    high_peak <- density_df |> filter(y == max(y))
    low_peak <- density_df |> filter(x < 15) |> filter(y == max(y))
    
    tibble::tibble(
      max_y_high = high_peak$y,
      x_at_max_y_high = high_peak$x,
      max_y_low = low_peak$y,
      x_at_max_y_low = low_peak$x
    )
    #returns values in tibble form
}
#needed to use {{}} as passing in the column names and not variable objects - Gemini was used, as it was initially causing errors

peak_maxes<- determine_density_maxes(seoul_bikes, peak, TRUE, temperature_c)
non_peak_maxes <- determine_density_maxes(seoul_bikes, peak, FALSE, temperature_c)
#followed the following guide: https://ianmadd.github.io/pages/PeakDensityDistribution.html

seoul_bikes |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = temperature_c, alpha = 0.1, colour = ifelse(peak == TRUE, "#384860", "#97a6c4"))) +
  geom_density(linewidth = 1) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = peak_maxes$x_at_max_y_high, linetype = "dashed", colour = "#384860") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = peak_maxes$x_at_max_y_low, linetype = "dashed", colour = "#384860") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = non_peak_maxes$x_at_max_y_high, linetype = "dotted", colour = "#97a6c4") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = non_peak_maxes$x_at_max_y_low, linetype = "dotted", colour = "#97a6c4") +
  theme_minimal() +
  scale_colour_identity(
    guide = "legend",
    labels = c("Peak", "Non-Peak")
    ) +
  guides(alpha = "none") +
  labs(
    x = "Temperature (c)",
    y = "Density",
    colour = "Peak Commuting Hour (7-9am or 6-7pm)",
    title = stringr::str_wrap("Temperature Distribution Comparison : Peak and Non-Peak Commuting Hours")
    #needed str_wrap to ensure the entire title shows on the plot
  )
```

The both graphs are almost overlapping. This means that peak and non-peak commuting hours overlap almost completely across the entire temperature range (-20-40°C).

This means that higher bike demand seen during working-day peak hours are actually driven by commuting behaviour, rather than due to peak hours occuring during warmer weather. In other words, temperature is not a confounding factor.

Both groups also have the same bimodal, with peaks between approximately 4-11°C and 21-22°C, and a small dip in between. This reflects Seoul's climate of long, hot summers and long, cold winters, where the autumn and spring seasons are shorter.

This also shows how Seoul's seasonal temperature cycles affect peak and non-peak hours relatively equally.

### Seasons vs. Rented Bike Count considering Holidays
```{r, echo = FALSE}
hourly_holiday_comparison <- seoul_bikes %>%
  group_by(seasons, holiday, hour) %>%
  summarise(
    avg_rentals = mean(rented_bike_count, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
   )

ggplot(hourly_holiday_comparison,
       aes(x = hour, y = avg_rentals,
           colour = holiday)) +
  # Used geom_line() instead of geom_col() because I'm now investigating how rentals change throughout the day.
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  # Used facet_wrap() for easier comparison
  facet_wrap(
    ~factor(seasons,
                      levels = c("Winter", "Spring",
                                 "Summer", "Autumn")),
    #added axes = "all_x" by asking GenAi because I wanted all graphs to have x-axis only the bottom 2 originally had it.
    axes = "all_x"
  )+
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(0, 23, 3)) +

  labs(
     title = "Hourly average bike rentals by season and type of holiday",
    x = "Hour of day",
    y = "Average number of bikes rented",
    colour = "Holiday type"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() 
```


I learned that the temperature and season variables play an important role in predicting bike rental demand in Seoul. Demand is highest during summer and lowest during winter, suggesting that temperature affects people’s willingness to cycle. In addition, on non-holidays, demand consistently peaks around 8 am and 6 pm, reflecting typical commuting hours, while on holidays demand tends to increase more gradually throughout the day. These patterns indicate that the relationship between time of day and bike rental demand varies depending on the season and whether it is a holiday.

Therefore, incorporating both these variables into our predictive model could improve its accuracy, and through further modeling  we could determine the individual impact of specific weather factors such as temperature, rainfall, and humidity.







### Precipitation vs. Rented Bike Count

#### Rainfall vs. Rented Bike Count
```{r, echo = FALSE}
rain_data <- seoul_bikes %>%
  filter(snowfall_cm == 0)

# Define precipitation bands
rain_data <- rain_data %>%
  mutate(
    rain_level = case_when(
      rainfall_mm == 0 ~ "0",
      rainfall_mm > 0 & rainfall_mm <= 1 ~ "(0, 1]",
      rainfall_mm > 1 & rainfall_mm <= 5 ~ "(1, 5]",
      rainfall_mm > 5 & rainfall_mm <= 10 ~ "(5, 10]",
      rainfall_mm > 10 ~ ">10"
    ),
    rain_level = fct_relevel(
      rain_level,
      "0", "(0, 1]", "(1, 5]", "(5, 10]", ">10"
    )
  )

# Rainfall box plot: exclude snow to isolate rainfall
ggplot(
  data = rain_data,
  mapping = aes(x = rain_level, y = rented_bike_count)
) +
  geom_boxplot(fill = "lightblue") +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(
    title = "Bike rentals by rainfall level",
    x = "Rainfall (mm)",
    y = "Hourly bike rentals"
  )
```

Median hourly rentals drop from 643 under dry conditions to 127 when rainfall is greater than 0 and up to 1 mm, a decrease of around 80%. Demand falls more for rainfall above 10 mm, but increases a little. This would mean a steep drop at the beginning and then small changes. Not a straight line drop.

#### Snowfall vs. Rented Bike Count
```{r, echo = FALSE}
snow_data <- seoul_bikes %>%
  filter(rainfall_mm == 0)

snow_data <- snow_data %>%
  mutate(
    snow_level = case_when(
      snowfall_cm == 0 ~ "0",
      snowfall_cm > 0 & snowfall_cm <= 1 ~ "(0, 1]",
      snowfall_cm > 1 & snowfall_cm <= 3 ~ "(1, 3]",
      snowfall_cm > 3 & snowfall_cm <= 5 ~ "(3, 5]",
      snowfall_cm > 5 ~ ">5"
    ),
    snow_level = fct_relevel(
      snow_level,
      "0", "(0, 1]", "(1, 3]", "(3, 5]", ">5"
    )
  )

# Snowfall box plot: exclude rain to isolate snowfall
ggplot(
  data = snow_data,
  mapping = aes(x = snow_level, y = rented_bike_count)
) +
  geom_boxplot(fill = "lightgrey") +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(
    title = "Bike rentals by snowfall level",
    x = "Snowfall (cm)",
    y = "Hourly bike rentals"
  )
```

Median hourly rentals drop from 643 under dry conditions to 127 when rainfall is greater than 0 and up to 1 mm, a decrease of around 80%. Demand falls more for rainfall above 10 mm, but increases a little. This would mean a steep drop at the beginning and then small changes. Not a linear decline.

### Behaviour of Temperature vs. Humidity whilst considering Rented Bike Count

### Behaviour of Rented Bike Count on Weekdays Compared to Weekends & Holidays

```{r}
seoul_bikes <- seoul_bikes %>%
  mutate(
    day_type = if_else(
      lubridate::wday(as.Date(date, format = "%d/%m/%Y"),
                      week_start = 1) >= 6 | holiday == "Holiday",
      "Weekend/Holiday",
      "Weekday"
    )
  )


```

```{r}

hour_profile <- seoul_bikes |>
group_by(day_type, hour) |>
summarise( 
mean_rented_bikes = mean(`rented_bike_count`,na.rm = TRUE),
.groups = "drop"
)

ggplot(hour_profile, aes(x = hour, y = mean_rented_bikes, colour = day_type)) +
geom_line() +
labs(x = "Hour", y = "Mean rented bikes", colour = "Day type"
) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(0, 23, by = 2)) +
theme_minimal()

hour_profile |>
group_by(day_type) |>
slice_max(mean_rented_bikes, n = 1)

```

The mean rented bike count on weekdays (working days) has two abrupt peaks at 8am and 6pm with its 6pm peak coming in at 1766 rentals on average, which can be equated to the fact that an average working day is 9am-5pm. The weekend and holiday mean rented bike count however follows a sinusoidal curve, with its peak coming at 5pm with a calculated mean of 1140 bike rentals. Both have a similar shape when the weekday peaks are disregarded so evidently the working day has an incredible effect on average bikes rented per hour.

## Modelling

### Simplified Dataset

Below is the first 10 rows of the clean data set we will be using for modelling:

```{r, echo = FALSE}
seoul_bikes_clean <- seoul_bikes |> 
  mutate(
    precipitation = ifelse(rainfall_mm > 0 | snowfall_cm > 0, 1, 0),
    is_weekend   = wday(dmy(date)) %in% c(1, 7),
    #hour_holiday = interaction(hour, holiday, sep = "_")
    hour = as.factor(hour)
  ) |> 
  select(
    rented_bike_count,
    #hour_holiday,
    hour,
    holiday,
    is_weekend,
    temperature_c,
    humidity_percent,
    seasons,
    precipitation
  )

seoul_bikes_clean |> 
  head(10)
```
### Linear Models

We will be considering two models, one where we interact hour and holiday together, and one where hour and holiday are separately considered in the model. 

The reason we are considering the interaction between hour and holiday for a model is because from our EDA we determined that the number of rented bikes given a specific hour behaves very differently when it is a holiday and when it is not. 

Considering their interaction may provide us with more accuracy in terms of predictions.

```{r, echo = FALSE}
set.seed(67)

seoul_bikes_clean_split <- initial_split(seoul_bikes_clean, prop = 0.80)

train_data <- training(seoul_bikes_clean_split)
test_data <- testing(seoul_bikes_clean_split)

seoul_bikes_rec_1 <- recipe(
  rented_bike_count ~ .,
  data = train_data
) |> 
  step_dummy(all_nominal(), -all_outcomes()) |> 
  step_interact(terms = ~ starts_with("hour_"):starts_with("holiday_")) |> 
  step_zv(all_predictors())

seoul_bikes_rec_2 <- recipe(
  rented_bike_count ~ .,
  data = train_data
) |> 
  step_dummy(all_nominal(), -all_outcomes()) |>
  step_zv(all_predictors())

seoul_bikes_mod <- linear_reg() |> 
  set_engine("lm")

seoul_bikes_wflow_1 <- workflow() |> 
  add_model(seoul_bikes_mod) |> 
  add_recipe(seoul_bikes_rec_1)

seoul_bikes_wflow_2 <- workflow() |> 
  add_model(seoul_bikes_mod) |> 
  add_recipe(seoul_bikes_rec_2)

seoul_bikes_fit_1 <- seoul_bikes_wflow_1 |> 
  fit(data = train_data)

seoul_bikes_fit_1 |> 
  tidy() |> 
  kable(
    caption = "Model 1: Linear Regression with Hour-Holiday Interaction (55 Terms)",
    digits = 2
  )

seoul_bikes_fit_2 <- seoul_bikes_wflow_2 |> 
  fit(data = train_data)

seoul_bikes_fit_2 |> 
  tidy() |> 
  kable(
    caption = "Model 2: Linear Regression without Interaction (32 Terms)",
    digits = 2
  )
```

Below is the expression of the first model (with each of the slopes rounded to 2 decimal places):

$$
\begin{aligned}
\widehat{\text{rented_bike_count}} &= 903.26 - 68.74 \times \text{is_weekend} + 20.38 \times \text{temperature_c} - 6.70 \times \text{humidity_percent} \\
&\quad - 247.01 \times \text{precipitation} - 80.61 \times \text{hour_holiday_X1_Holiday} - 99.72 \times \text{hour_holiday_X2_Holiday} + \dots \\
&\quad - 29.98 \times \text{hour holiday X0 No.Holiday} - 132.89 \times \text{hour holiday X1 No.Holiday} + \dots \\
&\quad - 66.15 \times \text{seasons_Spring} + 11.12 \times \text{seasons_Summer} - 283.33 \times \text{seasons_Winter}
\end{aligned}
$$

Below is the expression of the second model (with each of the slopes rounded to 2 decimal places):


$$
\begin{aligned}
\widehat{\text{rented_bike_count}} &= 728.63 -68.83 \times \text{is_weekend} + 20.48 \times \text{temperature_c} - 6.73 \times \text{humidity_percent} \\
&\quad - 245.86 \times \text{precipitation} - 99.47 \times \text{hour_X1} - 197.92 \times \text{hour_X2} + \dots \\
&\quad + 153.47 \times \text{holiday_No.Holiday} - 66.23 \times \text{seasons_Spring} + 10.31 \times \text{seasons_Summer} \\
&\quad - 282.22 \times \text{seasons_Winter}
\end{aligned}
$$

### Results and Residual Graphs of Predictions

Below are some summary statistics that compare the predicted values of models 1, 2 and the real rented_bike_counts.

```{r, warning = FALSE, message = FALSE, echo = FALSE}
seoul_bikes_pred_1 <- predict(seoul_bikes_fit_1, new_data = test_data) |> 
  bind_cols(test_data |> select(rented_bike_count))

seoul_bikes_pred_2 <- predict(seoul_bikes_fit_2, new_data = test_data) |> 
  bind_cols(test_data |> select(rented_bike_count))

tibble(
  `Model 1 Pred` = seoul_bikes_pred_1$.pred,
  `Model 2 Pred` = seoul_bikes_pred_2$.pred,
  `Real Bike Count` = test_data$rented_bike_count
) |> 
  tidy()
```

#### Evaluation Metrics
```{r, echo = FALSE}
bikes_metrics <- metric_set(rmse, rsq)

eval_model <- function(pred_df, wflow, model){
  std_metrics <- pred_df |> 
    bikes_metrics(truth = rented_bike_count, estimate = .pred) |> 
    select(.metric, .estimate) |> 
    pivot_wider(names_from = .metric, values_from = .estimate)
  
  n <- nrow(pred_df)
  p <- nrow(tidy(wflow)) - 1 #-1 because of the baseline
  min <- min(pred_df$rented_bike_count)
  max <- max(pred_df$rented_bike_count)
  
  std_metrics |> 
    mutate(
      model = model,
      num_terms = p+1, #+1 here as the total number of terms includes the baseline
      adj_rsq = 1 - ((1 - rsq) * (n-1)) / (n - p - 1),
      min = min,
      max = max
    ) |> 
    select(model, num_terms, rmse, min, max, rsq, adj_rsq)
}

bind_rows(
  eval_model(seoul_bikes_pred_1, seoul_bikes_fit_1, "Model 1"),
  eval_model(seoul_bikes_pred_2, seoul_bikes_fit_2, "Model 2")
) |> 
  kable(digits = 4, caption = "Model Evaluation Metrics (Testing Data)")
```

From the above table of evaluative metrics and by Occam's Razor, we will be choosing model 2 as our predictive model, as it involves way fewer terms and has similar performance, as seen from the differences in RMSE, r-squared and adjusted r-squared.

RMSE: 411.6669 - across test-set observations between 0 and 3404 bikes per hour, this value corresponds to roughly 12.1% of the total demand range.

R-Squared: 0.575 - 57.5% of variance in the hourly rented bike counts is explained by model 2 on our testing dataset.

#### Residual Graph

```{r}

ggplot(seoul_bikes_aug, aes(x = .pred, y = .resid)) +

     geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", color = "gray") +

     ) +

seoul_bikes_aug_test <- augment(
  seoul_bikes_fit_2,
  new_data = test_data)

ggplot(seoul_bikes_aug_test, aes(x = .pred, y = .resid)) +
     geom_point(alpha = 0.5) +
     geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", color = "gray") +
     labs(

```



## Limitations

1. **Bike-demand is non-linear** when considered with multiple variables within the dataset, e.g. temperature, hour of day, precipitation etc.

2. Combining variables for simplicity into a binary variable of the model, namely the use of precipitation **decreases the accuracy** of our model.

3. **Model can predict negative bike counts**, which are impossible, considering real values are above 0

4. **Omitted contextual variables**, e.g. public transport disruptions, major local events etc. leaves approximately 42.5% of variance unexplained.


## Generative AI Disclosure

Google Gemini was used during EDA, in particular when writing a reusable helper function for the density plots of temperature vs. density at peak and non-peak commuting hours. 

Additionally, it was also used for the bike demand vs. temperature graph for simplifying an if-statement.

When evaluating performance of the models, Google Gemini was used to aid the computation of adjusted r-squared and the formatting of the output of the metrics, for the tested data.
